610.title: Simhika
610.hook: flying fast over the sea, Hanuman suddenly slows down, and nothing seems to be holding him
610.howItsDone: In Sundara Kanda recitations, Simhika is remembered as the third of the beings Hanuman meets over the sea, and tellers often contrast her with Surasa, who tested him and blessed him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surasa, and a Hanuman the size of a thumb and your line, both are kept at once: her rule and his promise. Did you find a way where both sides kept their word? Today, the last meeting over the sea. Day six hundred ten.

Nothing is wrong, exactly. Hanuman is flying fast, Surasa's blessing behind him, the sea open ahead. He has met a mountain and a serpent mother out here, and both of them he could see. And then, all at once, his speed fails. He's being held back, Valmiki says, like a great ship against a contrary wind. No storm, no wall, no monster. Every stretch of air takes more effort than the last, and he can't see why. When he looks around, there's nothing there.
screen: `HIS SPEED FAILS.` → `LIKE A SHIP AGAINST THE WIND.` → `NOTHING THERE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman looks up, down, left, right. Then he looks below him, at the water, and he sees her. A huge creature has risen from the sea. Her name is Simhika, and she is a rakshasi, a demoness, and she has a particular power: she catches creatures by their shadows. She has seized Hanuman's shadow where it falls on the waves, and through it she is dragging him down. Hanuman realizes what she is. Valmiki says he remembers: this is the shadow-catching creature that Sugriva, the monkey king, had told them about before the search began. Sugriva had briefed his searchers on the dangers of each direction, and this was one of the southern ones. So the slowing wasn't weakness, and it wasn't his imagination. It had a name. Look at how the danger works. Simhika doesn't attack Hanuman. She attacks his shadow, the part of him that's down on the water, the part he isn't watching. And it's only when he stops looking ahead and looks down, at what's below and behind him, that he can see what's been holding him back. Notice, too, that Simhika is different from Surasa. Surasa was sent by the gods to test him and blessed him when he passed. Simhika is not a test. She simply wants to eat whatever flies over her water. Valmiki says she opens her mouth wide. And Hanuman, knowing exactly what he's facing now, gets ready.
screen: `HANUMAN LOOKS ALL AROUND.` · `SHE HAS SEIZED HIS SHADOW.` · `SUGRIVA HAD WARNED THEM.` · then, large: `NOT A TEST THIS TIME.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow. Think of something that's been slowing you down lately without a clear reason. Instead of pushing forward, do what Hanuman did: look around, and then look down. Ask gently: what's underneath this? Tiredness, a worry, an old habit, something someone said? You don't have to fix it. Just see if it has a name. Breathe with whatever you find. The bell holds the time.
Simhika. The rakshasi in the southern sea who catches flying creatures by their shadows, and drags Hanuman down until he looks below and recognizes her.
Your line: she has seized his shadow. Today, when something drags without reason, stop and look underneath before pushing harder. Day six hundred ten.

611.title: Simhika
611.hook: three meetings over the sea, three different answers, and then the far shore
611.howItsDone: Readers of the Sundara Kanda often point to the verse about steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill as a summary of Hanuman's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Simhika, and your line, she has seized his shadow, which dragged him down until he looked below and knew her. Did you look underneath something that was dragging? Today, what he does about her. Day six hundred eleven.

A good doctor doesn't treat every patient the same way. A good teacher doesn't answer every question with the same tone. Knowing which response a moment needs is a skill all its own. Over this one stretch of sea, Hanuman has now met three beings. One offered him rest. One tested him. And one, Simhika, wants to swallow him whole. Same monkey, same crossing, same stretch of water. Watch how differently he answers each.
screen: `WHICH RESPONSE DOES THIS NEED?` → `REST, A TEST, A THREAT.`

segments.voice: Simhika opens her mouth wide, and Hanuman does what worked with Surasa, at first. He makes himself huge, and she opens wider. Then he makes himself small and drops straight into her mouth. But this time he doesn't dart back out with a bow. Inside her, Valmiki says, he tears at her vital organs with his nails, and then he shoots out again, quick as thought. Simhika falls dead into the sea. The beings watching from the sky cheer. And Valmiki gives them a line worth keeping. Whoever has, as you do, four things, they say, steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill, does not fail at the work. Now set the three meetings side by side. Mainaka offered a gift, and Hanuman answered with courtesy: a touch of the hand, a thank-you, and onward. Surasa set a test from the gods, and he answered with wit: smaller, not bigger, and both promises kept. Simhika was simply a danger, and he answered with force, quickly and completely. Same Hanuman, three very different responses. That's those four qualities in action. Steadiness, to stay on course. Insight, to see what each thing really is. Intelligence, to choose the right move. Skill, to carry it out. Then Hanuman looks ahead and sees it at last: the far shore. Trees, a line of hills, and beyond them a city. He comes down on a mountain at the water's edge. Valmiki notes that after a hundred yojanas, he isn't even out of breath.
screen: `INTO THE MOUTH, AND OUT AGAIN.` · `STEADINESS, INSIGHT, MIND, SKILL.` · `COURTESY, WIT, FORCE.` · then, large: `THE FAR SHORE.`

segments.voice: Think back over yesterday. Find three moments that asked something different of you: one that needed kindness, one that needed cleverness, one that needed firmness. For each, notice what you actually gave. No grading. Just see it. Then let the breath come and go, steady, as Hanuman lands without being out of breath. The bell holds the time.
Simhika. The shadow-catcher whom Hanuman defeats from the inside, the third of three meetings over the sea, each answered in a different way.
Your line: steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill. Today, before you respond to something, ask: is this a gift, a test, or a threat? Day six hundred eleven.

612.title: Lanka by night
612.hook: the bravest monkey in the army looks at the golden city and decides to wait until dark, and to be the size of a cat
612.carry: a swan gliding on a lake
612.howItsDone: Storytellers telling the Sundara Kanda often dwell on Hanuman's careful reasoning before entering Lanka, and on his choice to go in small, by night.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Simhika, and your line, steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill, the four seen in three meetings answered with courtesy, wit and force. Did you ask whether something was a gift, a test or a threat? Today, the far shore. Day six hundred twelve.

Hanuman is standing on a hilltop at the edge of the sea, and in front of him is Lanka. Valmiki paints it from his eyes. A city on a mountain, ringed with golden walls, moats full of water, gates with guards, towers that seem to touch the clouds. Banners. Gardens. It is breathtaking. And it is, very obviously, a fortress. The monkey who just crossed an ocean in one leap stands still and thinks.
screen: `A CITY ON A MOUNTAIN.` → `GOLDEN WALLS, GUARDED GATES.` → `HANUMAN STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: What Hanuman thinks about is not how strong he is. It's how easily he could ruin everything. Valmiki lets us hear his reasoning. This city is guarded by rakshasas everywhere. If I'm seen in my own form, there'll be a fight, and even if I win it, Ravana will know Rama has found him, and Sita may be moved or harmed. A messenger who acts without thinking, he reasons, can wreck the very thing he was sent to do. So his plan is the opposite of a hero's entrance. He'll wait for night. He'll make himself small, Valmiki says the size of a cat, and slip in unseen. And he'll search the whole city, house by house, until he finds her. So he waits. The sun goes down over Lanka. And then he shrinks and makes for the city. And just as he sets out, the moon rises. Valmiki gives it a picture: the moon in the sky like a swan gliding on a lake, its light falling on the city as if to help him. After the leap across the sea, the next heroic act is patience. Waiting for dark. Choosing to be small. Courage in the Sundara Kanda isn't only the jump. It's knowing when to make yourself unnoticeable, so the real work can be done. Tomorrow, someone at the gate notices anyway.
screen: `HOW EASILY HE COULD RUIN IT.` · `WAIT FOR NIGHT; BE CAT-SIZED.` · `THE MOON RISES LIKE A SWAN.` · then, large: `THE NEXT HEROIC ACT IS PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Let yourself grow still. Imagine dusk falling: the light dimming, sounds softening. Make yourself small for a moment, not in a sad way, just quiet and light, the way Hanuman waits on the hill. There's nothing to prove right now. Let the breath be low and easy. If you'd like, picture a moon rising slowly, giving just enough light to see by. The bell holds the time.
Lanka, Ravana's island city, which Hanuman enters only after sunset, shrunk to the size of a cat, as the moon rises like a swan gliding on a lake.
Your line: a swan gliding on a lake. Today, before you charge into something, pause and ask what would make it go wrong, and plan around that. Day six hundred twelve.

screen: `DAY 612 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LANKA BY NIGHT, PART TWO.`

613.title: Lanka by night
613.hook: the city itself steps out to stop Hanuman, and then, once he's inside, the enemy's capital turns out to be full of music
613.carry: do what you came to do
613.howItsDone: Readers of the Sundara Kanda often note how richly Valmiki describes Lanka, and the encounter with the city's guardian is a well-known episode in recitations and dance-dramas.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lanka, part one. Hanuman waited for dark, made himself the size of a cat, and your line, a swan gliding on a lake. Did you plan around what could go wrong? Today, inside the walls. Day six hundred thirteen.

A city at night is never one sound. It is a hundred small ones. Someone practicing piano. A couple arguing. A party. A night-shift worker locking up. A kid reading under a lamp. Before Hanuman can hear any of that in Lanka, though, he has to get past the gate. And at the gate, a figure steps out of the dark. She is huge and fierce, and she asks what a monkey is doing here.
screen: `A DOZEN LIVES AT ONCE.` → `A FIGURE AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: She is Lanka herself, the guardian spirit of the city, sometimes called Lankini. She blocks his way, mocks him, and strikes him. Hanuman hits back, but holds himself in. Valmiki says he uses only his left fist, and not with full force, because she is a woman. Even so, she falls. And from the ground she says something extraordinary. Long ago, she tells him, Brahma, the creator, warned me: when a monkey overpowers you, know that the end of the rakshasas has come. So go in, she says. Do what you came to do. Then Hanuman is inside, and Valmiki opens the city to us. This is not a cartoon villain's lair. Hanuman passes mansions bright with lamps. He hears singing and the sound of instruments. He hears, from some houses, the Vedas being chanted. He sees lovers, and people drinking, and warriors with their weapons, and guards on their rounds, and some rakshasas who are graceful and some who are frightening. Valmiki describes the city with real admiration. Ravana's Lanka is wealthy, beautiful, learned and alive. Hold on to that. Here the epic doesn't pretend that the other side is ugly or empty. The city that holds Sita captive is full of music and prayer and ordinary people living their lives. It makes Ravana's wrong sharper, not softer. And it makes Hanuman's task much harder: somewhere in all this light and noise, one woman is grieving, and he has to find her without being seen.
screen: `LANKA HERSELF AT THE GATE.` · `HE STRIKES WITH HIS LEFT FIST.` · `BRAHMA'S OLD WARNING.` · then, large: `A CITY FULL OF MUSIC AND PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let your attention go to sound. Listen to everything you can hear right now, near and far: a fridge, traffic, birds, your own breath. Don't name or judge the sounds. Just let them be many lives happening at once, the way Hanuman hears Lanka. Then, among all of them, find one quiet sound and rest your attention there. The bell holds the time.

Rakshasa, the beings of Ravana's city, one of whom, the guardian Lanka herself, falls to Hanuman's blow and lets him pass inside, where the capital is full of lamps, music, and the chanting of the Vedas.
Your line: do what you came to do. Today, notice one good thing about a place or person you'd rather not like. Day six hundred thirteen.

614.title: Ravana's palace
614.hook: in the most splendid room in Lanka, Hanuman sees a beautiful queen asleep and thinks, for one wild moment, that his search is over
614.carry: he knew her character before he knew her face
614.howItsDone: Readers of the Sundara Kanda often smile at Hanuman's leap of joy over Mandodari, and commentators point to how he recognizes his mistake by reasoning about Sita's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rakshasa, part two. The city's guardian fell and let him in, and inside, a capital full of music and prayer. Your line was do what you came to do. Did you notice one good thing about a place you'd rather not like? Today, the center of it all. Day six hundred fourteen.

All night Hanuman has searched Lanka house by house, and every house has been the wrong one. Now he reaches the heart of the city, Ravana's own palace, glittering and guarded, and slips inside. And there, in the innermost room, he sees a woman so beautiful and so regal that his heart leaps. After a hundred yojanas of sea and a city full of strangers, he's sure he has found her. He's about to celebrate too soon.
screen: `HOUSE BY HOUSE, ALL NIGHT.` → `THE INNERMOST ROOM.` → `HE'S SURE.`

segments.voice: Valmiki takes his time getting us there. First Hanuman sees the Pushpaka, the flying chariot, made by the divine craftsman Vishvakarma, which Ravana took from his own half-brother Kubera. It's covered in jewels and seems to float. Then he enters a vast hall where Ravana's many wives lie asleep after a night of music and wine, their ornaments scattered, like a lake of lotuses closed for the night. Then Ravana himself, asleep on a magnificent bed, enormous and powerful. And near him, on a separate couch, a woman lovelier than all the rest, adorned and serene. Hanuman's joy explodes. Valmiki says he slaps his arms, kisses his tail, runs about, sings, climbs the pillars and jumps down again. He's a monkey, and for one moment he behaves like one, wildly happy. Then he stops. And thinks. Sita, separated from Rama, he reasons, would not be sleeping peacefully. She wouldn't wear jewels. She wouldn't eat and drink at a banquet. She would never lie in another man's palace content. This is not Sita. The woman is Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen. It's a small scene, and a funny one, but notice what it shows. Hanuman's first impression was wrong, and he corrected it not by looking harder at her face. He had only glimpsed Sita once, far off in the sky, as Ravana carried her past Sugriva's mountain. He corrected it by thinking about who Sita is. Her grief, her faithfulness, her love for Rama. He knew her character before he knew her face. That's what he'll recognize her by.
screen: `THE PUSHPAKA, THE FLYING CHARIOT.` · `A HALL OF SLEEPING QUEENS.` · `HANUMAN'S WILD JOY.` · then, large: `SITA WOULD NOT SLEEP LIKE THIS.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of someone you love, and instead of picturing their face, think of how they are: the way they laugh, what they'd do when sad, what they'd never do. Let those qualities come one at a time with each breath. Notice that you'd know them by these even in a crowd, even with your eyes closed. Rest with them there. The bell holds the time.
Ravana's palace. The flying chariot, the hall of sleeping queens, and Mandodari, whom Hanuman mistakes for Sita until he remembers who Sita is.
Your line: he knew her character before he knew her face. Today, before you celebrate or panic, take one breath and check it against what you actually know. Day six hundred fourteen.

615.title: Ravana's palace
615.hook: having searched every room, Hanuman sits down in the dark and considers giving up, and then talks himself back up
615.howItsDone: Some who recite the Sundara Kanda in hard times dwell on Hanuman's despair and recovery here, and on the phrase anirvedaḥ śriyo mūlam, 'not despairing is the root of good fortune'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's palace, part one. The flying chariot, the sleeping queens, and Mandodari, mistaken for Sita for one joyful moment. Your line was he knew her character before he knew her face. Did you check something before celebrating? Today, the low point. Day six hundred fifteen.

Sometimes the hardest moment isn't the danger. It's the end of the list. You've looked everywhere you can think of, called everyone, tried every option, and nothing. Hanuman has now searched Ravana's palace from end to end, room after room. He hasn't found her. The night is wearing on. And he sits down. Valmiki gives the hero of the Sundara Kanda something surprising here: a full, honest spell of despair.
screen: `THE END OF THE LIST.` → `HANUMAN SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: First comes a moment of conscience. Hanuman realizes he has walked among sleeping women, other men's wives, and looked at them. Has he done wrong? He thinks it through. His mind, he decides, was not disturbed. He looked only because a woman must be searched for among women, and his intention was pure. Valmiki lets him weigh it rather than skip it. Then the despair. Maybe Sita is dead, he thinks. Maybe the rakshasas killed her. Early in it, Valmiki gives him a line in Sanskrit: anirvedaḥ śriyo mūlam. Not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune. He searches again, cellars, halls, corners. Still nothing. And the despair comes back, deeper. If I go back without news, what happens? Rama will die of grief, then Lakshmana, then Bharata, then Rama's mothers, and on through Sugriva. He follows the chain of sorrow all the way down. For a while he even thinks of not going back at all, of staying by the sea and living as a hermit. And then, slowly, he turns. He bows in his heart to Rama and Lakshmana, to Sita, and to the gods, and he begins again. Notice that the line didn't settle it once and for all. Hanuman said it, and still fell further. The line is about what he did next, each time. Despair came and sat with him, and he didn't let it make the decision. And so this part of the story ends with him looking out from the palace walls at a grove of trees he hasn't entered yet.
screen: `A MOMENT OF CONSCIENCE.` · `THE CHAIN OF SORROW.` · `ANIRVEDAH SHRIYO MULAM.` · then, large: `HE GETS UP AND SEARCHES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. If there's something you've been close to giving up on, let it come to mind gently. Don't argue with the discouragement. Let it sit beside you, the way Hanuman's despair sat with him. Breathe with it. Then, on one breath, just notice: is there one place you haven't looked yet? One small next step? You don't have to take it now. Just let it appear. The bell holds the time.
Ravana's palace. Where Hanuman searches every room and finds no Sita, sinks into despair, and rises again: not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune.
Your line: the root of good fortune. Today, when you hit the end of the list, look for one place you haven't searched yet. Day six hundred fifteen.

616.title: the ashoka grove
616.hook: the grove's name means without sorrow, and in the middle of it sits the saddest person in Lanka
616.howItsDone: Sita in the Ashoka grove is a familiar scene in Ramayana painting and performance, and some devotees, reciting this part of the Sundara Kanda, slow down at the moment Hanuman first sees her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's palace, part two. Every room searched, despair, and then the line: not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune. Did you find one place you hadn't looked yet? Today, Hanuman finds his. And the week looks back. Day six hundred sixteen.

There's a tree in South Asia called the ashoka. Its name in Sanskrit means without sorrow: a, not, and shoka, sorrow. It flowers red and orange, and people plant it in gardens for its beauty. Ravana has a whole grove of them beside his palace, a pleasure garden full of flowering trees, birds and streams. Birdsong, water, shade. And when Hanuman leaps over its wall, he's about to find a name that says the opposite of what it holds.
screen: `ASHOKA: WITHOUT SORROW.` → `A PLEASURE GARDEN.` → `A NAME AND ITS OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman climbs a tall shimshapa tree, thick with leaves, near a clear pool. He reasons it out: if Sita is here, she'll come to this water for her prayers at dawn. So he hides in the branches and watches. And then he sees her. Valmiki describes her slowly, the way you'd describe someone you'd waited a long time to see. She is thin from fasting. She wears a single, faded garment. She sits on the ground, sighing, surrounded by rakshasis with fierce faces. Valmiki gives two pictures: she is like a flame veiled in smoke, and like the thin crescent moon behind clouds. The light is still there; it's just covered. How does Hanuman know it's her? Not from her face, which he had only glimpsed far off in the sky. From her ornaments: the ones she wears match those Rama described, and the ones missing are the ones she dropped on the mountain as Ravana carried her away. And from her grief, which is exactly what he reasoned Sita's would be, back in the palace. Valmiki says Hanuman weeps, there in the tree. So this is where a long week ends. It began with Simhika catching his shadow over the sea, and Hanuman reaching the far shore not out of breath. Then Lanka by night: the guardian at the gate, the city of music and prayer. Then Ravana's palace: the flying chariot, Mandodari mistaken for Sita, every room searched, despair and recovery. And now, in the grove called without sorrow, sorrow itself, sitting on the ground. Found.

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone you know who seems fine on the outside but may be carrying something heavy: a light veiled in smoke. You don't need to know the details. Just hold them in your mind, quietly, the way Hanuman watches from the branches without intruding. Breathe in for them; breathe out for them. Let your care be steady and unhurried. The bell holds the time.
Ashoka, the tree, and Ravana's grove of them, whose name means without sorrow, where Hanuman, hidden in a shimshapa tree, finally sees Sita, thin, grieving and guarded, and weeps.
Your line: a flame veiled in smoke. Today, send a quiet word to someone who might be grieving behind a calm face. Day six hundred sixteen.
